html:
Communication is about more than just exchanging information. It's about understanding the emotion and intentions behind the information. Effective communication is also a two-way street. It’s not only how you convey a message so that it is received and understood by someone in exactly the way you intended, it’s also how you listen to gain the full meaning of what’s being said and to make the other person feel heard and understood.

More than just the words you use, effective communication combines a set of skills including nonverbal communication, engaged listening, managing stress in the moment, the ability to communicate assertively, and the capacity to recognize and understand your own emotions and those of the person you’re communicating with.

Effective communication is the glue that helps you deepen your connections to others and improve teamwork, decision making, and problem solving. It enables you to communicate even negative or difficult messages without creating conflict or destroying trust. 
​
While effective communication is a learned skill, it is more effective when it’s spontaneous rather than formulaic. A speech that is read, for example, rarely has the same impact as a speech that’s delivered (or appears to be delivered) spontaneously. Of course, it takes time and effort to develop these skills and become an effective communicator. The more effort and practice you put in, the more instinctive and spontaneous your communication skills will become.
TOP ISSUES THAT BREAKDOWN COMMUNICATION:
  • Not really listening. 
  • Being condescending.  
  • Speaking before thinking.
  • Only talking about what you want to talk about.
  • Raising your voice.
  • Negative non-verbal communication. (Facial and Body Language)
  • Speaking in superlatives. (Always/Never)
  • Being judgmental.
  • Blame-shifting.
  • Not trying to understand.
  • Unfaithfulness.
Learn to Communicate

It sounds so simple: say what you mean. But all too often, what we try to communicate gets lost in translation despite our best intentions. We say one thing, the other person hears something else, and misunderstandings, frustration, and conflicts ensue. 
​
Fortunately, you can learn how to communicate more clearly and effectively. Whether you’re trying to improve communication with your spouse, kids, boss, or coworkers, you can improve the communication skills that enable you to effectively connect with others, build trust and respect, and feel heard and understood.
​
Although this is not 100%, statistics say that:

A man's communication revolves around negotiation.
To preserve independence, seek to win, avoid failure, avoid taking orders, seek control and asymmetry, are adversarial with conflicting goals, mainly to transmit information or offer advice.

A woman's communication revolves around connection.
Conversations are negotiations for closeness, to preserve intimacy and avoid isolation.  Women are generally okay with taking orders if it is perceived to increase understanding.  Women prefer equality and symmetry as well as value similarity.  Woman's main goal is to maintain interaction.

Mental health professionals have found that communication problems were cited as the most common factor
​that leads to divorce (65 percent),
followed by couples' inability to resolve conflict (43 percent)​

title: Relationship Coaching
description: Relationship Coaching with Sherée Bergman: build understanding, strengthen communication and boundaries, and work toward healthier connections through faith-centered support.
html:
Build understanding, strengthen communication, and create healthier connections.

Your relationships influence nearly every part of your life. Yet even people who care deeply about one another can struggle to communicate, work through disagreements, or feel understood.

When misunderstandings become familiar patterns, you may feel dismissed, disconnected, or alone—even when you are together. These struggles can affect your confidence, emotional well-being, family life, and relationships at work.

Relationship Coaching offers a supportive space to understand what is happening, recognize your needs, and explore healthier ways of connecting with others.

What Is Relationship Coaching?

Relationship Coaching helps individuals and couples work toward more respectful, fulfilling relationships. Through thoughtful questions, practical tools, encouragement, and accountability, coaching supports you in identifying concerns, setting goals, and practicing new skills.

Whether you are navigating marriage, parenting, blended-family challenges, friendships, or workplace relationships, you can explore where communication breaks down, how expectations differ, and what patterns may be keeping you disconnected.

What You Can Learn

  • Express your feelings and needs clearly without relying on blame or criticism.
  • Listen to understand rather than preparing your next response.
  • Recognize how you give and receive care and communicate what helps you feel valued.
  • Approach disagreements constructively while respecting each person’s boundaries.
  • Respond to stress more intentionally and recognize when a conversation needs a pause.
  • Offer meaningful apologies that acknowledge harm, accept responsibility, and lead to changes in behavior.
  • Understand recurring patterns and explore how past experiences may influence present interactions.
  • Explore forgiveness and trust while honoring accountability, safety, and your readiness.
  • Set realistic goals and take manageable steps toward healthier connections.

How Coaching Can Help

As you develop these skills, you can work toward:

  • Greater self-understanding about your needs, values, strengths, and responses.
  • Stronger connection through honest conversations and shared goals.
  • Deeper emotional closeness where mutual trust and respect are present.
  • More constructive conflict resolution that makes room for feelings without allowing hurtful behavior.
  • Greater compassion while maintaining clear boundaries.
  • Healthier interactions with your partner, children, extended family, friends, and colleagues.
  • Support through challenges as you consider your choices and practice meaningful changes.

A Faith-Centered Approach to Restoration

At Heart to Heart, restoration includes emotional, relational, and spiritual growth. Coaching offers room to explore wounds from the past, recognize protective patterns, and consider how those patterns affect your relationships today.

Through prayer, biblical reflection, and practical coaching tools, Sherée encourages you to deepen your relationship with God and grow in Christlike love, honesty, compassion, and responsibility.

Restoration does not mean ignoring harm, abandoning boundaries, or carrying the responsibility for another person’s choices. It can involve rebuilding a relationship when both people are willing to participate—or finding healing and direction when reconciliation is not possible or safe.

Moving Forward with Understanding and Hope

Every relationship has its own history, strengths, and challenges. Coaching gives you an opportunity to pause, reflect, and take thoughtful steps toward change.

You can change how you communicate and respond, but you cannot make another person participate or treat you respectfully. Lasting relationship growth requires mutual effort, honesty, and care. When abuse or coercive control is present, safety and individual support take priority over improving communication together.

Heart to Heart Life Coaching offers personalized support to help you understand your relationship challenges, strengthen communication, and make choices that honor your needs and values.

The goal is to help you move forward with greater self-understanding, clearer boundaries, and hope for healthier relationships.

title: Smartphones
description: The way you use your mobile device around your family can affect your relationships. Cell phones can make you feel more connected, but they also can…
html:
The way you use your mobile device around your family can affect your relationships. Cell phones can make you feel more connected, but they also can distract you and your family from connecting with each other in person. While some people need to check their phones for work or emergency purposes, it’s important to model and prioritize making meaningful connections through face-to-face communication.  

​We live in a world where communication through modern technology is almost required.  Everywhere people are texting, emailing, checking social media, writing blogs and tweeting.  It’s hard to go anywhere without seeing someone using a phone or the Internet to connect with others. In some ways, our phones help us create and maintain relationships: They help you find companionship, let people look into the eyes of family and friends who can't be with them, and connect lovers across vast expanses of land and sea.  Still, the use and even presence of a smartphone during in-person interactions can lessen the quality of those moments.  

Let’s take for example two individuals in a relationship. If the couple spends more time communicating and spending time through texting, there is a loss of affection in the relationship. They miss out on the intimacy of actually spending quality face to face time with someone. Conversations can become misinterpreted, which can lead to ‘drama’ and relationship/friendship problems. Texting and social media allows people to hide behind screens and to not truly express themselves for who they are.  The unspoken subtext of checking text messages in front of friends is: “Somewhere else there is someone who I care about more than you. I want to know what they have to say more than what you have to say to me now.” The idea of being present in the moment is disappearing. Quality time with friends and family suffers.  But before you know it or realize it, you might be using a good chunk of the time you're supposed to be spending with your partner or children focusing on your phone instead of on your family.  And considering how busy families are today, all the time we spend on phones is a heavy price to pay. "The more precious your time is, the more you need to be vigilant about how you spend it.

​Statistics show that it erodes our relationships, our interaction with our spouse and children and our relationships are not as good as we may think. We may picture ourselves as multitasking machines, doing a good job with everything all at the same time. But what we may not realize is that attention has limited capacity.  When you're with someone and you're on the phone at the same time, you are where the phone is—in the virtual world.  It's not quantity; it's quality.  If you're with your child for five hours but you are on the phone constantly during that time, it's not really spending time with them.   And kids agree.  An annual survey conducted by the children's magazine Highlights found that 62% of kids aged 6 to 12 said their parents are distracted when trying to talk to them, with cell phone use being the top culprit.  Think about how it feels to be ignored—it's certainly not a feeling you'd wish on your children.

We have enough things that interfere with our family time—busy work schedules, homework, extracurricular activities. Research shows that many people often lose track of time when they're on their cell phones (understandable considering how many things we can do on these devices, from checking news and sports scores to seeing what friends are posting on social media sites, not to mention getting email and texts). When you spend time on the phone, you have that much less time to spend fully engaging and giving your attention to your spouse and kids. The other thing to consider when you're a parent who is constantly connected to their phone,  kids learn by watching what we do. Even young children, more of whom are getting cell phones at younger ages, are likely to pick up on the way a parent might engages with their phone and adopting that behavior.

Clearly, texting is the preferred method of communication among young people, and that trend is moving upward toward adults, who are also texting much more frequently. Teens are in the stage of their life where they’re learning so if you don’t learn to have good communication skills, then when you become an adult you will have a harder time asking for help, being proactive with things in your life and knowing how to have good face-to-face relationship in life.  There is also the complaints that our new digital skills impact our ability to write properly.  Studies show that homework is interrupted and children become distracted when they receive notifications of a new chat messages, texts, or emails.

What happens when we become too dependent on our mobile phones?  We lose our ability to have deeper, more spontaneous conversations with others, changing the nature of our social interactions in alarming ways. Technology is making us feel more and more isolated, even though it promised to make us more connected. Because conversation is the most human and humanizing thing that we do. It’s where empathy is born, where intimacy is born—because of eye contact, because we can hear the tones of another person’s voice, sense their body movements, sense their presence. It’s where we learn about other people. But, without meaning to, without having made a plan, we’ve actually moved away from conversation in a way that research is showing is it's hurting us. How are cell phones and other technologies hurting us? 88% of Americans say that during their last social interaction, they took out a phone, and 82% said that it deteriorated the conversation they were in. Basically, we’re doing something that we know is hurting our interactions.  Studies show if you put a cell phone into a social interaction, it does two things: First, it decreases the quality of what you talk about, because you talk about things where you wouldn’t mind being interrupted, which makes sense, and, secondly, it decreases the empathic connection that people feel toward each other.  So, even something as simple as going to lunch and putting a cell phone on the table decreases the emotional importance of what people are willing to talk about, and it decreases the connection that the two people feel toward one another.

Our cell phones make us promises that are like gifts from a benevolent genie—that we will never have to be alone, that we will never be bored, that we can put our attention wherever we want it to be, and that we can multitask, which is perhaps the most seductive of all. That ability to put your attention wherever you want it to be has become the thing people want most in their social interactions. Actually allowing yourself a moment of boredom is crucial to human interaction and it’s crucial to your brain as well—that feeling that you don’t have to commit yourself 100 percent and you can avoid the terror that there will be a moment in an interaction when you’ll be bored. When you’re bored, your brain isn’t bored at all—it’s replenishing itself, and it needs that down time. We’re very susceptible to cell phones, and we even get a neurochemical high from the constant stimulation that our phones give us. ​Our poor brains!
Cell phone use while driving has become a growing danger: Texting and cell phone use has been shown to dramatically increase the chances of motor vehicle accidents leading to injury and even death.

  • Driving while texting causes 1.6 million car accidents in the US every year.
  • You are 20 times more likely to crash while texting and driving than you are when not using a cell phone (Virginia Tech)
  • Texting while has the same effect on your driving reaction time as if you had consumed four beers in a single hour (Drivesafeonline.org)
  • Texting distracts you long enough to travel the length of an entire football with your eyes off the road, driving at 55 mph (Drivesafeonline.org)
  • 35% of teens admit to texting and driving, even though 94% of them understand the dangers (AAA)
  • 1 in 4 teens admit to responding to at least one text every time they drive (AAA)
  • 10% of parents and 20% of teens admit to having multi-text conversations while driving (AAA)
  • Teens who text while driving spend an average of 10% of their driving time outside of traffic lanes (Drivesafeonline.org).
  • 20% of US drivers reported sending emails or text messages while on the road.
  • 25% of all car crashes in the US involved the use of a cell phone.
We can still change!  We can use our phones in ways that are better for our kids, our families, our work, and ourselves. The path ahead is not a path where we do without technology, but of living in greater harmony with it. Some first steps we can create sacred spaces—the kitchen, the dining room, the car—that are device-free and set aside for conversation. When you have lunch with a friend or colleague or family member, don’t put a phone on the table between you. Make meals a time when you are there to listen and be heard AND BE IN THE PRESENT.

Once you’ve given some thought to your own cell phone use (and what you might be modeling for your family), think about your own rules you want your family to follow when you’re together.

No more saying "yes" when my heart is saying "no".

Heart to Heart Life Coaching recognizes that violence is rising at an alarming rate.
1 in every 3 women have experienced abuse in their life time.
1 in every 10 men have experienced abuse in their life time.
It is stated that domestic violence is the leading cause of death and injury in the United States.

There is no race, age, sexual orientation, gender, religious affiliation, educational background or socioeconomic level that domestic abuse and domestic violence does not affect.

Emotional abuse is not always easy to recognize. The abusive person may appear kind, charming, and caring to others while behaving very differently in private. Behind closed doors, their partner or family members may experience intimidation, humiliation, manipulation, threats, or violence. This difference between public behavior and private treatment can leave those experiencing abuse feeling confused, isolated, and unsure whether others will believe them.

Recognizing emotional abuse can be especially painful when you remember the affection and connection you once shared—or still experience between hurtful episodes. You may find yourself hoping that the caring behavior will return. Emotional attachment, financial concerns, children, faith, fear, and safety concerns can make decisions about the relationship complicated. Difficulty leaving does not mean you accept the abuse, and the abuse is never your fault.

Abuse can take many forms, including emotional, psychological, physical, sexual, financial, and spiritual abuse. Neglect and controlling behavior can also cause lasting harm. Emotional abuse deserves to be taken seriously, even when there are no visible injuries. Repeated criticism, humiliation, manipulation, isolation, and efforts to undermine your sense of reality can erode your confidence, self-trust, and sense of safety.

Some abusive behaviors may overlap with traits commonly described as narcissistic, such as entitlement, exploitation, and a lack of empathy. However, abusive behavior alone does not establish a diagnosis. You do not need a label or diagnosis to recognize harmful treatment or seek support.

YOUR ABUSIVE PARTNER DOESN’T THINK THEY HAVE A PROBLEM WITH THEIR ANGER;
THEY HAVE A PROBLEM WITH YOUR ANGER FOR THE TERRIBLE WAY THEY TREAT YOU!

Emotionally abusive behavior can leave you feeling as though you are not allowed to be angry about the way you are being treated. The person hurting you may expect you to remain calm and quiet while treating their own anger as justified. When you express hurt or frustration, they may shift attention away from their behavior and focus entirely on your reaction.

Sherée calls this “STARTING IN THE MIDDLE.” Instead of acknowledging what led to your anger, the story begins with your response—as though it happened without a cause. Your reaction may then be used to portray you as unreasonable or overly emotional, while the treatment that prompted it goes unaddressed.

Over time, feeling pressured to silence your emotions can leave you feeling trapped, unheard, and disconnected from yourself. You may begin questioning whether your feelings are valid or whether you have the right to speak up. Your anger deserves to be understood. It can signal that you have been hurt, that a boundary has been crossed, or that something needs attention. You deserve space to acknowledge those feelings and choose how to respond in ways that support your safety and well-being.

“You’re too sensitive” can become another way of dismissing your experience. When you hear it repeatedly, you may start doubting your perceptions instead of recognizing the impact of someone else’s behavior.

Sensitivity is not a flaw. It can be a capacity for empathy, awareness, and meaningful connection. You do not have to become less sensitive to deserve respectful treatment. Your feelings deserve consideration, and your concerns deserve to be heard.

title: Emotional Abuse Coaching
description: Faith-centered Abuse Recovery Coaching for understanding your experiences, rebuilding self-trust, strengthening boundaries, and taking steps toward healing.
html:
Abuse Recovery Coaching

Faith-centered support for understanding what you’ve experienced, rebuilding self-trust, and taking meaningful steps toward healing.

If a difficult relationship has left you feeling confused, unheard, emotionally exhausted, or unsure of yourself, you are not alone. Emotional abuse can affect your confidence, your ability to trust, and your sense of safety in relationships. You may recognize that something has been wrong while still struggling to understand what happened or what to do next.

Abuse Recovery Coaching offers a compassionate, nonjudgmental space to explore your experiences, recognize harmful patterns, and begin reconnecting with your feelings, needs, and values. You do not need to have every answer—or know exactly where to begin—to seek support.

Making sense of your experience

Emotional abuse can be especially isolating when the behavior you experience in private is very different from what others see. Manipulation, blame, criticism, emotional withdrawal, gaslighting, control, or repeated cycles of affection and rejection may leave you asking:

  • Was it really abuse?
  • Why did I stay?
  • Why do I still miss them?
  • Why do I keep questioning myself?
  • Why am I afraid to trust again?
  • Why do familiar patterns keep appearing in my relationships?

Coaching gives you room to explore these questions without judgment or pressure to make decisions before you are ready. You do not need a label or diagnosis for the other person to recognize that their behavior has hurt you.

Understanding relationship and attachment patterns

Alongside recognizing abusive behavior, you may want to explore how earlier experiences influence your relationships today. Our earliest connections can shape what feels familiar, how we respond to closeness or conflict, and what we expect from others.

Understanding these patterns is never about blaming yourself for someone else’s behavior. The responsibility for abuse belongs to the person choosing abusive behavior. Exploring your own experiences can help you understand your needs, recognize your choices, and build healthier ways of relating.

What coaching can support

Through thoughtful questions, practical tools, reflection, and encouragement, we can explore:

  • Recognizing harmful patterns and making sense of confusing experiences.
  • Rebuilding self-trust by reconnecting with your feelings, perceptions, and values.
  • Understanding emotional triggers and practicing more intentional responses.
  • Strengthening boundaries and learning to express your needs.
  • Exploring attachment wounds and their influence on present relationships.
  • Making room for grief over the relationship you experienced or hoped to have.
  • Developing healthier communication while recognizing that you cannot control another person’s choices.
  • Drawing on your faith for comfort, wisdom, and encouragement.
  • Taking manageable steps forward that respect your circumstances, safety, and readiness.

Support at your own pace

You may still be trying to understand what is happening in your relationship. You may have recently left, or you may have been out of the relationship for years and begun recognizing wounds that still need care.

Wherever you are, coaching offers space to feel heard and consider what moving forward could look like for you. You can share at your own pace, pause when you need to, and work toward changes that reflect your needs.

What happened to you does not have to define the rest of your story. There is room for understanding, renewed self-trust, healthier connections, and hope for the chapters ahead.

This is where healing begins with understanding, and you don’t have to walk the journey alone.

SCHEDULE AN APPOINTMENT

title: Start at Start to Finish Strong
description: Explore Start at Start to Finish Strong by Sherée Bergman, a personal, faith-centered perspective on past experiences, emotional wounds, and healing.
html:
Start at Start to Finish Strong invites you to explore how the experiences of your past may still be shaping your life today—and how understanding those connections can become a meaningful part of your emotional and spiritual healing journey.

Have you ever wondered why certain situations affect you so deeply, why familiar struggles keep showing up in your relationships, or why moving forward feels difficult even when you want things to change? Sometimes the answers begin earlier in your story. Childhood experiences, relationships with caregivers, and needs that went unmet can influence what you believe about yourself, what you expect from others, and how you respond when you feel hurt, afraid, or rejected.

Through personal storytelling, biblical reflection, and insights drawn from her own healing journey, Sherée Bergman explores the lasting effects of emotional wounds. She shares how pain carried from childhood followed her into adulthood, where it continued to affect her choices, relationships, and sense of worth. With honesty about both her struggles and her growth, she offers readers encouragement to begin looking at their own stories with greater understanding and compassion.

At the heart of the book is an invitation to start at the start: to consider where painful beliefs and protective patterns may have begun. Responses that once helped you cope—such as withdrawing, trying to please everyone, staying constantly on guard, or putting your own needs aside—may eventually leave you feeling disconnected or stuck. Recognizing these patterns creates an opportunity to understand what you have been carrying and consider a different way forward.

The book encourages you to explore:

  • The connection between childhood and adult life. Consider how early experiences may influence your beliefs, emotional responses, and relationships today.
  • The effects of unmet emotional needs. Reflect on how a lack of consistent comfort, affection, acceptance, or security may have shaped the way you see yourself and others.
  • The beliefs beneath familiar struggles. Begin noticing messages you may have absorbed about your worth, your needs, and whether it is safe to trust.
  • The patterns you developed to protect yourself. Understand those responses with compassion while considering whether they still support the life and relationships you want.
  • The role of faith in your healing journey. Explore what it means to bring your pain, questions, and beliefs before God and make room for His comfort and guidance.
  • The possibility of meaningful change. Recognize that understanding your past can help you approach the present with greater awareness and choice.

Faith is woven throughout Sherée’s story. She describes how her relationship with Jesus Christ became a source of strength and hope through painful seasons, and how healing unfolded over time. Her story reflects the courage it can take to acknowledge hurt, receive support, question long-held beliefs, and learn to trust again.

This book does not ask you to pretend the past never happened or pressure you to have everything figured out. It invites you to acknowledge your experiences honestly, recognize their influence, and take your next steps at a pace that respects your needs. Starting at the beginning is an opportunity to understand your story more fully and discover what may still need care.

For readers who want to explore these themes more personally, the companion Start at Start Transformation Guide offers structured reflection and exercises. The Breakthrough Journal provides space to examine emotionally difficult moments and recognize connections between present reactions and earlier experiences. Together, these resources offer different ways to engage with the ideas introduced in the main book.

Whether you are beginning to recognize the effects of earlier wounds or have already spent time exploring your story, Start at Start to Finish Strong offers a personal, faith-centered perspective on emotional healing. Sherée’s message is one of hope: your pain deserves to be acknowledged, your story matters, and your past does not have to define every chapter ahead.

Some clients require more structure, some seek more guidance and some simply need more accountability and encouragement. What exactly does that mean?  It means get ready to roll up your sleeves and get to work on the things that are holding you back from having true happiness in your relationship(s) and life.  A key focus of their work is to adapt their approach for each individual and find their "Glass Walls" so they can be different once and for all.   They specialize in guiding their clients to achieve results in a most authentic way.

title: Motivation
description: Have you ever felt a bit lost? Not quite sure what it is you want to do with your life? Or do you know what you want to do but it's hard to find…
html:
Have you ever felt a bit lost?  Not quite sure what it is you want to do with your life?  Or do you know what you want to do but it's hard to find motivation to do the things you need to do to get started.  When we lack motivation, everything can feel difficult.  

​What motivation really is..... 
Motivation comes from within ourselves.  It is our purpose or reason for doing something.  Our motivation for something stems from our values and beliefs.  When you have a strong sense of your personal values and beliefs, it forms a basis from which your motivation can go.

​We all have different motivators.  Some have an inner mission of wanting to help others.  Some may include personal power, career success and money.  Neither is wrong, however, many find external motivators like money or perceived success less powerful and we experience burn-out. Internal motivators alignment with our core values and the energy seems endless.

Something that really pushes our motivation button is accountability.  Telling someone about your dreams and having them check in with you to see how you are doing on your plan of action.

What is the difference between motivation and inspiration?  Someone can give a motivational speech but what they really are doing is inspiring their audience.  True motivation actually come from within ourselves.  Inspiration comes from the outside world.  Speakers, writers, mentors, coaches and others can inspire us.   Movies, music, books and art can do that also.

Picture motivation to be the fire in your belly, your purpose, your WHY...then picture inspiration as the fuel for that fire.  The two work together.  Inspiration can certainly be a tool to help increase your motivation but can not replace what was put in you in the first place.  

Empowerment Coaches are very good at helping you find that fire that you lost or never even discovered.

title: F.A.Q.
description: Answers to questions about getting started, Christian coaching, emotional healing, relationships, support groups, appointments, and fees.
html:
Getting Started

What is the first step in getting started?

We highly recommend scheduling a FREE 20-Minute Discovery Phone Call before booking your first coaching session.

This complimentary conversation gives us an opportunity to learn about your needs, answer your questions, discuss your goals, and determine whether our coaching services are the right fit for you.

We want to make sure you understand what to expect and choose the services that will best support your needs before making a financial commitment.

Please note: Coaching appointments are nonrefundable once booked, subject to our published appointment policies and applicable law. We encourage you to review these policies before scheduling.

Schedule Your FREE Discovery Phone Call

How do I know if coaching is right for me?

Coaching may be a wonderful next step if you recognize that something in your life needs to change but aren't sure how to move forward.

Perhaps you feel stuck, overwhelmed, discouraged, or uncertain about your future. You may be struggling with relationships, repeating unhealthy patterns, or longing for greater peace, confidence, and purpose.

Two important ingredients for a successful coaching relationship are:

  • Awareness: You recognize a difference between where you are today and where you would like to be.
  • Willingness: You are open to learning, personal growth, and taking meaningful steps toward change.

You don't need to have all the answers before beginning. Sometimes, discovering those answers is part of the journey.

What if I don't know why I feel stuck or unhappy?

You don't have to know exactly what's wrong or have a clear plan before coming to coaching.

Sometimes you simply recognize that something in your life isn't working. You may feel unfulfilled, discouraged, disconnected, or caught in patterns you don't understand.

Through thoughtful conversation and guided self-reflection, we can work together to identify areas of concern, explore possible contributing factors, and discover meaningful next steps.

When can I begin coaching?

You can begin as soon as an appointment is available.

We encourage you to start with a complimentary Discovery Phone Call. However, if you already know that coaching is right for you, you may schedule your first appointment directly.

View Availability and Schedule an Appointment

Our Christian Coaching Approach

Is your coaching Christian-based?

Yes. Our coaching approach is rooted in Christian faith and biblical principles.

We believe that lasting spiritual growth and meaningful personal transformation are deeply connected to understanding God's truth, discovering our identity in Christ, and learning to live according to His wisdom.

We incorporate Scripture, prayer, and biblical guidance into the coaching process because we believe that Jesus Christ is the ultimate source of truth, hope, and spiritual restoration.

We recognize that each person's spiritual journey is unique, and we approach every individual with compassion, understanding, and respect.

Do I have to be a Christian to receive coaching?

You do not have to be a Christian to benefit from practical coaching tools, greater self-awareness, healthier communication, and personal development.

However, our approach is grounded in Christian values, and we want clients to understand that faith is an important part of our coaching philosophy.

We welcome the opportunity to work with individuals from different backgrounds while remaining faithful to the biblical principles that guide our work.

During your complimentary Discovery Phone Call, we can discuss your preferences and determine whether our approach is a comfortable fit for you.

How does faith in Jesus Christ relate to emotional healing?

We believe that true spiritual healing begins with Jesus Christ, who offers hope, truth, grace, forgiveness, and restoration.

Many people carry emotional wounds that have influenced the way they see themselves, relate to others, and even understand God's love for them.

Our Christian approach recognizes the importance of identifying these wounds, understanding their influence, renewing unhealthy beliefs through God's Word, and discovering our true identity and worth in Christ.

Healing does not mean pretending the past never happened or denying the pain we have experienced. Instead, we believe God invites us to bring our brokenness to Him and walk forward in His truth, wisdom, and love.

Spiritual healing and professional mental health care can complement one another when additional support is needed.

Can I incorporate prayer and Scripture into my coaching sessions?

Absolutely! Prayer, Scripture, and biblical wisdom are central to our coaching philosophy.

We believe that seeking God's guidance, understanding His truth, and deepening our relationship with Him can be powerful parts of personal growth and spiritual transformation.

We encourage clients to bring their questions, concerns, and struggles into their relationship with God as they seek wisdom and direction for their lives.

Understanding Life Coaching

What is a Life Coach?

A Life Coach is a trained professional who partners with you to help you gain clarity, overcome obstacles, develop healthier patterns, and move toward the life you desire.

Your coach provides a compassionate, nonjudgmental environment where you can explore your thoughts, feelings, values, strengths, relationships, and personal goals.

Through meaningful conversations, thoughtful questions, encouragement, practical tools, and gentle accountability, coaching can help you:

  • Discover your strengths, values, gifts, and spiritual purpose.
  • Recognize limiting beliefs and unhealthy patterns.
  • Develop greater self-awareness and confidence.
  • Improve relationships and communication skills.
  • Establish healthy boundaries.
  • Build a more balanced, intentional, and fulfilling life.

Coaching is a partnership. You remain in control of your choices, goals, and pace of progress. Your coach walks alongside you, offering encouragement, insight, and support throughout the process.

What areas of my life can coaching help with?

Coaching can be beneficial in many areas of life, including relationships, communication, personal growth, confidence, self-worth, boundaries, life transitions, decision-making, and discovering your spiritual purpose.

Some clients come with a specific goal, while others know something needs to change but aren't quite sure where to begin.

Together, we can explore the areas where you feel stuck and identify meaningful steps toward the changes you desire.

Can coaching help me if I'm going through a difficult season?

Yes. Life can bring unexpected challenges, painful experiences, broken relationships, and seasons of uncertainty.

Coaching can provide encouragement, perspective, practical strategies, and a supportive environment as you work through decisions and determine your next steps.

If your circumstances require mental health treatment, crisis intervention, or specialized clinical care, we may recommend working with an appropriately licensed professional, either instead of or alongside coaching.

How is Life Coaching different from counseling or therapy?

Although coaching and counseling can complement one another, they serve different purposes.

Life coaching focuses on personal growth, self-awareness, goals, decision-making, developing new skills, and taking meaningful steps toward change.

Counseling or psychotherapy is provided by qualified mental health professionals and may include diagnosing and treating mental health conditions, addressing psychological symptoms, and providing clinical trauma treatment.

Our coaching services are not a substitute for licensed mental health care.

We recognize that past experiences can influence present-day beliefs, behaviors, and relationships. When appropriate, coaching may include exploring those connections to help you develop greater awareness and make healthier choices.

Why do people choose to work with a Life Coach?

Many people reach a point in life when they begin asking deeper questions:

  • Who am I, really?
  • Why do I keep repeating the same patterns?
  • Why do I feel stuck or unfulfilled?
  • How can I improve my relationships?
  • What is holding me back from becoming who I want to be?
  • What is God's purpose for my life?

Working with a coach provides dedicated time to explore these questions with someone who can offer a fresh perspective, encouragement, structure, and accountability.

Sometimes, having someone walk alongside you can make a meaningful difference.

Emotional Healing and Understanding Your Past

Can coaching help me understand how my past affects my present?

Yes. Many of the beliefs, emotional responses, and relationship patterns we carry into adulthood were influenced by our earlier life experiences.

You may find yourself struggling with people-pleasing, fear of rejection, low self-worth, difficulty setting boundaries, or repeatedly entering unhealthy relationships without fully understanding why.

Through compassionate self-reflection and increased awareness, coaching can help you recognize these connections and begin making healthier choices in the present.

For deeper emotional concerns or trauma-related symptoms, licensed mental health care may also be appropriate.

Why is it important to address emotional wounds from childhood?

Childhood is a foundational season of life when we begin developing beliefs about ourselves, others, relationships, and the world around us.

When our emotional needs are not adequately met, we may develop unhealthy beliefs about our worth, lovability, safety, or acceptance.

These beliefs can follow us into adulthood, influencing our decisions, emotional responses, self-confidence, and relationships—sometimes without our realizing it.

Becoming aware of these patterns can be an important first step toward replacing unhealthy beliefs with truth and developing healthier ways of living.

From a Christian perspective, we also believe that understanding our identity in Christ and renewing our minds through God's Word are essential parts of spiritual growth and healing.

Why do I keep repeating the same unhealthy patterns?

Sometimes we repeat patterns because they became familiar to us through earlier experiences, relationships, or beliefs.

For example, someone who learned that love and acceptance depended on pleasing others may continue sacrificing personal needs to gain approval.

Another person who experienced repeated criticism may grow into adulthood believing they are never good enough.

These patterns do not have to define your future.

Through greater awareness, biblical wisdom, and intentional choices, you can begin challenging unhealthy beliefs and developing new ways of responding to life and relationships.

Can emotional healing help improve my relationships?

Understanding your emotional wounds and recognizing unhealthy relationship patterns can help you develop greater self-awareness, healthier boundaries, and stronger communication skills.

As you grow in emotional maturity and learn to respond differently, you may begin experiencing positive changes in the way you relate to others.

However, healthy relationships require responsibility, respect, and appropriate effort from everyone involved. Your personal growth does not guarantee that another person will change.

Does forgiveness mean I have to reconcile with someone who has hurt me?

No. Forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same thing.

From a Christian perspective, forgiveness involves releasing resentment and the desire for revenge, while entrusting justice to God.

Forgiveness does not mean excusing harmful behavior, denying what happened, automatically restoring trust, or allowing someone to continue mistreating you.

Reconciliation requires mutual willingness, accountability, and meaningful change.

You can pursue forgiveness while maintaining healthy boundaries and protecting yourself from further harm.

Relationships, Boundaries, and Emotional Abuse

Can coaching help me if I've experienced narcissistic or emotional abuse?

Experiencing emotional or narcissistic abuse can leave you feeling confused, rejected, emotionally exhausted, or unsure of your own judgment.

Coaching can provide a compassionate environment to help you recognize unhealthy relationship patterns, rebuild self-trust, strengthen boundaries, improve communication, and regain a sense of personal direction.

Our approach also recognizes the importance of understanding how earlier emotional wounds may influence the relationships we form and the behaviors we tolerate.

While coaching does not replace trauma therapy, crisis support, or other specialized professional services, it may be a valuable part of your journey toward greater emotional well-being and healthier relationships.

Why do I keep finding myself in unhealthy relationships?

Sometimes we unknowingly repeat familiar relationship patterns because of beliefs and emotional experiences formed earlier in life.

For example, someone who grew up feeling unworthy of love or acceptance may become accustomed to working excessively hard to please others, overlooking their own needs, or tolerating unhealthy behavior in relationships.

Understanding these patterns can help you develop greater self-awareness, recognize your worth, and begin making different choices.

You cannot change your past, but you can change how you respond to its influence on your present and future.

Can you help me learn to set healthy boundaries?

Yes. Healthy boundaries are an important part of developing self-respect, emotional well-being, and healthier relationships.

Coaching can help you recognize where boundaries are needed, communicate your needs more clearly, and learn how to respond when others do not respect your limits.

Setting boundaries is not about controlling another person. It is about taking responsibility for your own choices, behavior, and well-being.

Healthy boundaries can also be consistent with Christian love, forgiveness, and compassion.

Can coaching help me rebuild my confidence and self-worth after an unhealthy relationship?

Yes. Repeated criticism, rejection, manipulation, or emotional mistreatment can gradually undermine your confidence and cause you to question your judgment and worth.

Coaching can help you recognize the harmful messages you may have come to believe, develop greater self-awareness, rebuild confidence in your decisions, and establish healthier expectations for relationships.

From a Christian perspective, we also encourage you to discover your worth and identity in who God created you to be rather than allowing another person's treatment of you to define your value.

Can you help me decide whether to stay in or leave an unhealthy relationship?

We understand that relationship decisions can be deeply personal, emotional, and sometimes complicated.

Our role is not to make those decisions for you, but to help you explore your circumstances, recognize unhealthy patterns, clarify your values, understand your options, and make more informed decisions.

We believe every individual deserves to be treated with dignity and respect.

If you are experiencing threats, coercive control, or physical danger, specialized domestic abuse services and appropriate safety planning should take priority.

Support Group for Women Experiencing Narcissistic and Emotional Abuse

Do you offer a support group for women experiencing narcissistic or emotional abuse?

Yes! We offer a Christian-based support group for women who have experienced narcissistic or emotional abuse, whether they are currently in an unhealthy relationship or are working toward healing after leaving one.

We recognize that these experiences can leave women feeling isolated, confused, rejected, and emotionally wounded.

Our support group provides a compassionate and supportive environment where women can share their experiences, gain understanding, receive encouragement, and begin discovering a path toward healing and renewed hope.

Learn More About Our Women's Support Group

Do I have to be a Christian to attend the support group?

No. Women from different backgrounds are welcome.

However, our support group is Christian-based, and biblical principles, spiritual encouragement, and faith in Jesus Christ are important parts of our approach to healing.

We believe that God desires to restore what has been wounded and that His truth, love, and wisdom can bring lasting hope.

Every woman is treated with compassion and respect, regardless of where she is in her spiritual journey.

Do I have to share my personal story in the support group?

No. Sharing your personal experiences is always your choice.

We understand that discussing painful or deeply personal situations can feel overwhelming, especially when you are just beginning to recognize or process what you have experienced.

Some women find comfort in sharing their stories, while others prefer to listen until they feel more comfortable.

Our goal is to create a respectful environment where you can participate at a pace that feels appropriate for you.

What can I expect during a support group meeting?

Our meetings provide opportunities for meaningful discussion, encouragement, learning, and connection with women who may understand experiences similar to yours.

We explore topics related to narcissistic and emotional abuse, unhealthy relationship patterns, boundaries, emotional wounds, personal growth, and healing through Christ.

Depending on the meeting, there may be a short teaching, guided discussion, opportunities for personal sharing, and prayer.

Our goal is for women to leave feeling heard, encouraged, better informed, and reminded that they do not have to walk through their healing journey alone.

Is the support group the same as group therapy?

No. Our support group is a peer-support and educational environment guided by Christian principles. It is not group psychotherapy or a substitute for professional mental health treatment.

The group is designed to provide understanding, encouragement, connection, biblical guidance, and practical information to support personal growth.

Women who need specialized trauma treatment, clinical mental health services, or crisis intervention are encouraged to seek appropriately qualified professional care.

Will what I share in the support group remain confidential?

We take privacy seriously and ask participants to respect the confidentiality of the women who attend.

Group guidelines address the importance of not sharing another participant's personal experiences or identifying information outside the meetings.

However, no group can guarantee absolute confidentiality, and there may be legal or safety-related exceptions. Participants should use discretion when sharing sensitive information.

Our goal is to foster an atmosphere of trust, respect, and emotional safety. Here is the link to see our Group Confidentiality and Disclaimer Agreement Group Confidentiality and Disclaimer Agreement

How can I learn more about joining the support group?

We would love for you to learn more about the group and determine whether it may be a good fit for your needs.

You can find additional information about the group's purpose, meeting details, and how to express your interest on our dedicated support group website.

Visit Our Women's Support Group Website

What to Expect During Coaching

What can I expect during a coaching session?

Each coaching session is personalized to your needs, concerns, and goals.

We begin by listening carefully to understand what you are experiencing and what you hope to accomplish.

Depending on your individual needs, sessions may include thoughtful questions, exploring beliefs and behavior patterns, identifying obstacles, discussing practical strategies, and developing an action plan.

Our goal is to create an atmosphere where you feel heard, respected, supported, and encouraged to grow.

What methods and tools do you use in coaching?

We use a variety of coaching tools and techniques tailored to your individual needs.

These may include guided self-reflection, questionnaires, books and workbooks, spiritual strengths assessments, communication exercises, role-playing, practical scripts, real-life scenarios, goal setting, and action planning.

We may also recommend exercises, journaling, or other activities between sessions to help you apply what you've learned.

Our approach combines compassion, encouragement, honest feedback, practical guidance, and accountability. We believe personal growth should be meaningful, empowering, and sometimes even enjoyable!

When appropriate, we may also explore whether our Emotional Healing services would be beneficial.

Will I have activities or assignments to complete between sessions?

Sometimes. Depending on your goals and the areas we are working on, we may recommend journaling, workbook exercises, personal reflection, communication exercises, Scripture study, or practical action steps between appointments.

These activities are intended to help you apply what you are learning in everyday life.

Meaningful growth often takes place not only during coaching sessions but also through the choices and changes you make between them.

Is what I share during coaching confidential?

We understand that personal growth and emotional healing often involve discussing sensitive experiences and deeply personal concerns.

We are committed to treating your information with care, professionalism, and respect.

Our coaching agreement explains our confidentiality practices and any applicable legal, ethical, or safety-related limitations.

We encourage you to review those terms and ask questions before beginning coaching.

Appointments and Scheduling

How long are coaching appointments?

Our standard coaching sessions are 60 minutes.

If you would like additional time, longer sessions may be arranged based on availability.

To schedule two consecutive appointments, please contact our office directly.

How often should I schedule coaching sessions?

We generally encourage clients to begin with weekly sessions for several consecutive weeks. Meeting consistently helps establish momentum, build trust, and support meaningful progress.

As you begin reaching your goals, you may choose to meet less frequently, continue with regular appointments, or conclude your coaching relationship.

Your schedule can be adjusted according to your needs, goals, and availability.

How long will I need to work with a coach?

Every person's needs and goals are different.

Some clients benefit from just a few sessions to work through a specific situation or decision. Others have more extensive goals and find that a commitment of three to six months provides the time and consistency needed for meaningful progress.

There is no required long-term commitment. You are always an active participant in deciding the direction and duration of your coaching journey.

Where are coaching sessions held?

We offer convenient options so you can receive coaching from a private, comfortable location.

Phone Coaching: Enjoy the convenience of coaching from your own home or another location of your choice.

Learn About Phone Coaching

Virtual Coaching: We also offer video sessions through Zoom or FaceTime.

Learn About Virtual Coaching

Distance does not have to be a barrier to receiving encouragement, guidance, and support.

What if I need to cancel or reschedule an appointment?

We understand that unexpected circumstances arise and sometimes appointments need to be changed.

We ask that you provide at least 72 hours' notice whenever possible.

Appointments are subject to our cancellation and rescheduling policy, which explains the requirements for making changes and any applicable fees or restrictions.

Please review these terms before scheduling.

View Our Cancellation and Rescheduling Policy

Fees, Payments, and Insurance

How much does coaching cost?

We offer a FREE 20-Minute Discovery Phone Call so you can learn more about our services and determine whether we are the right fit for you before making a financial commitment.

Session fees and additional information about our coaching services are available on our website.

View Coaching Services and Fees

Do you accept insurance?

No. Our life coaching services are private-pay and are not billed to health insurance.

Life coaching is not the same as licensed mental health treatment and is generally not covered by health insurance plans.

What forms of payment do you accept?

We accept PayPal and major debit and credit cards, including Visa, Mastercard, Discover, and American Express.

We do not accept personal checks.

How do I schedule and pay for my appointments?

You can conveniently view available appointments, schedule your session, and submit payment through our online booking system.

Schedule and Pay for Your Appointment

If you prefer, you may also contact our office to arrange your appointment.

All appointments must be paid in full before the scheduled session.

Are coaching appointments refundable?

Coaching appointments are nonrefundable once booked.

We strongly encourage you to schedule a complimentary Discovery Phone Call before booking your first session so you can make an informed decision about our services.

If you need to change an appointment, rescheduling requests are handled according to our Cancellation and Rescheduling Policy. A nonrefundable appointment does not necessarily mean that the appointment cannot be rescheduled under that policy.

Review Our Cancellation and Rescheduling Policy

Choosing the Right Coach

What qualifications should I look for in a Life Coach?

Choosing the right coach is an important personal decision.

Look for someone who has received reputable training, holds relevant certifications, demonstrates strong listening and communication skills, and has experience in the areas where you need support.

Just as importantly, look for someone who demonstrates compassion, integrity, respect, and the ability to offer honest feedback without judgment.

Above all, you should feel safe, heard, respected, and comfortable with your coach.

Our complimentary Discovery Phone Call provides an opportunity to ask questions, discuss your expectations, and determine whether our coaching relationship would be a good fit.

How do I know if you're the right coach for me?

The right coaching relationship is built on trust, mutual respect, open communication, and a shared understanding of your goals.

You should feel comfortable expressing your thoughts and concerns, asking questions, and discussing difficult subjects without fear of judgment.

We encourage you to take advantage of our complimentary Discovery Phone Call to get acquainted, share what you're looking for, and decide whether our approach aligns with your needs.

We would be honored to hear your story and explore how we might help you move forward.

Schedule Your FREE 20-Minute Discovery Phone Call

Ready to Take the First Step?

You don't have to have everything figured out before reaching out.

Whether you are seeking personal growth, healthier relationships, emotional healing, or a deeper understanding of God's purpose for your life, we would be honored to walk alongside you.

Healing is possible. Your story is not over. There is hope for your future.

html:
Teenage Stress

The teenage years can be some of the most awesome and challenging times of life!  The emotional and hormonal changes can make everything feel exaggerated and out of balance which can feel like a roller coaster ride on a rainy day.  

​A Los Angeles Times report showed that teens have a harder time saying no to drugs and/or pier pressure when they lack family bonding.  Many teens who take drugs or use alcohol say they don't feel loved.  They feel detached and afraid.  It doesn't necessarily mean that they aren't loved but it's how they feel.  Other teens say they are escaping a sense of hopelessness about life.  These aren't the only reasons teenagers use drugs and alcohol, but they are major factors that teens themselves are reporting.  Divorce has also taken its toll on family bonding.  Studies show that nationwide, 60% of youngsters feel they are to blame in a divorce and feel rejected by at least one parent; 50% live in families where at least one of the divorced parents stayed angry.   One third of these children never see one of their parents again after divorce.  Teenagers often go to school or out into the world carrying emotional baggage from unresolved issues from home.

We can't afford to ignore the statistics on what is happening in today's society.  Basic survival is tougher, requiring much more energy - both parents needing jobs, children being raised at day care, 24% of all children living with only one parent who has to work, keep house and pay the bills.  A recent Los Angeles Times poll revealed that parents feel frustrated and guilty because they lack time to supervise their children.  78% of parents polled gave themselves a C, D or F grade in teaching their children moral values.  Another national survey found that 1 in 5 teenagers had not had a 10-minute conversation with a parent in the past month.  Overall, parents in today's world spend 10-12 fewer hours per week with their teenagers than parents did in the 60's.  The irony is that those of us who were teenagers in the 60's realize how much less time we spent with our parents compared to previous generations.

If these statistics don't apply, our child could also get involved with someone who does come from these realities…..which will affect them and their children if any. 

​So how can busy parents and adults bond with teens and inject more quality care into their already demanding schedules?  Time may not always be the real issue.  It's what parents and adults choose to do with the time they have.  Most parents do care, but their care gets diluted by their own lack of mental and emotional self-management.  Becoming "Heart Smart" is an effective facilitator for overcoming this dilemma.  Learning how to listen to each other from the heart with sincere attention is the first step.  Most people just listen to each other from the head, with their own thoughts and emotions running through their minds at the same time.  This goes for teenagers and adults as well.  This causes gaps in communication, leading to judgments, resentments and distance between people.

Working with teens with self-discovery creates a joint venture between their head and their heart so that they can manage their life and be who they really are.  When their head and hearts are out of sync, it leads to insecurity, inner turmoil and conflict with others.  When their head and hearts are in balance, it leads to creative problem-solving, self-security and esteem.   

Sherée is helping teens understand and manage their reactions to life and make their own healthy, positive choices on how to deal with relationships, temptations, resentments and boredom.   But also helping teen and parents relationships - bridging the communication gaps.
Building a joint venture between your head and your heart to "Become Your True Self"
​Consider making an appointment with Heart to Heart Life Coaching.
Invest in Yourself

html:
Narcissism 

Childhood:
Learned manipulative behaviors from parents, severe emotional and/or physical abuse, unpredictable or unreliable caregiving from parents, narcissistic parent(s), excessive praise for good behavior or excessive criticism for bad behavior; which leads to shame and false guilt, major trauma from separation/attachment, severe emotional neglect; which is another form of abuse. These can be just some of the things the child had experienced.  
 
Adulthood:
Lack of empathy, underlying sense of entitlement, exaggerated self concern, unable to have deep relationships, constant denial of damages they inflicted, themselves – if they do admit, its at a very minimal emotional level, destructive and self-defeating in marriages, failure to recognize others emotions, feelings and needs – especially closer relationships, fragile self-esteem but "appear" self confident and unemotional – except for anger, trouble keeping healthy close relationships.
 
Narcissistic personality disorder is much more prevalent in males than females.  Narcissists can typically have borderline personality, anxiety and depression from childhood.  They have a tendency to be “workaholics” especially if they have success and are good at what they do.  This is filling, again, that void from their childhood to build their self-esteem and/or avoid the realities of their outside emotional life.  They also are known to use stimulants to escape the “emotional realm” like, drugs, alcohol, gambling, sports, television, video games, etc.  They often have had pornography issues because this is a fantasy relationship that they can control in their mind and there is no risk; which also can give them a fixation with masturbation because it gives them physically what they need without the burden of “emotional connection”.  Extra marital affairs are prevalent because it boosts their self-image and is noncommittal; even if they have a loving spouse.  

Description:
People who are overly narcissistic commonly feel rejected, humiliated and threatened when given constructive criticism.  To protect themselves from this “perceived danger”; they react with disdain, blaming others, anger/rage and denial and shun the ones trying to help them.  Subconsciously, people are things to be used for their benefit to fill the lack of emotional needs that weren’t met as a child.  They eventually sabotage or destroy their good/close relationships and often isolate themselves and keep their surface relationships so they won’t be lonely (again, another form of using).  Personal male/female relationships are usually at a surface level because this would require them to be vulnerable and that is “perceived danger”.  Narcissists generalized that all are harmful and cannot be trusted.  They create a false persona as a protective barrier – like a false identity. 

No matter how skilled an extreme a narcissist is, they have a major “attachment dysfunction”.  The extreme narcissist is frozen in childhood in the emotional/relational area. They become emotionally stuck at the time of their major trauma of separation/attachment.  Typically, their emotional age and maturity corresponds to the age they experienced their major trauma. This trauma was devastating to the point that it almost killed that child emotionally. The pain never was totally gone and the bleeding was continuous. In order to survive, this child had to construct a protective barrier that insulates themselves from the external world of people. They generalized that all people are harmful and cannot be trusted.  They are very defensive and self-protective.
 
The protective insulation barrier that they constructed is called a false persona. They create a false identity. This identity is not the true person inside. The many types of false personas or identities that an extreme narcissist creates can vary.

Some narcissists may have the ability to change into a “variety” of identities according to the situation. The wounded child inside may choose to present a front as a tough individual. They may even look, by appearance, intimidating and scary to the average person. (walking around with a scowl)  They could also play the “nice guy/person” whom everyone likes.  A corporate type version can be one that is diplomatic, proper and appearing to care but in reality does not. They only care what people think about themselves; which falsely fills their lack of self-esteem.  Another very likeable extreme narcissist can be the one that chooses the comedian role.  But all-in-all they usually shut down and put up the thick wall.

Narcissists try to sustain an image of perfection and personal invincibility (which can appear prideful) for themselves and attempt to project that impression to others.  They will sidestep your questions with joke or making you suddenly forget what you were asking. Narcissists can be very skilled at dodging and ducking questions they don’t want to answer. If you press them, they will then “slot” you as “unsafe” and will begin to avoid you.  
 
People with narcissistic personality disorder often display condescending or patronizing attitudes. For example, they treat you like you don’t know much and talk to you like you are a beginner on subjects you already know.  This is also a conscious or subconscious way of building up their own self-esteem.  They can be unreasonable in their expectations. Example, they may emotionally hurt someone (often the case) and expect the other person to just move on and get over it. They are “unwilling” to recognize or identify with the feelings and needs of others. 
 
There is also the success-oriented narcissist. They will be your friend and keep you close to themselves (so it appears) as long as you are useful.  They can be giving but it will be always from a non-emotional level using material things to make you think they care.  If you have needs emotionally, then the narcissist will avoid you.  It does not matter that you have helped the narcissist in their critical moments of their life; they lack empathy for you.

Is there hope for even an extreme narcissist living in the “emotional and relational fort” of isolation.  Is a narcissist able to have a healthy life? Definitely!  Some extreme narcissists have become very healthy in their emotional and relational lives but it took hard work. They typically don't think they are the problem so usually don't seek help unless they are in a place of devastation; which is the biggest reason why many are not healed.  Also, they have a tendency to quit when the going gets tuff, especially when the focus is change.  Having to change would dismantle their corrupted belief system of their ideal of who they "think" they are.  They also like being in control so change is not an area they usually want to enter because they would have to put themselves in a vulnerable place.

The first step is to find competent help that knows how to heal childhood emotional traumas through the help of the Holy Spirit. Just because a counselor may have all kinds of credentials it does not mean they are competent in dealing effectively with childhood trauma issues in this way. Sometimes the person has blocked out horrible memories and the Holy Spirit can bring these memories forth but in a way that does not traumatize the person.   Because extreme narcissists have an early history of emotional wounds, they are full of distrust.  If they can get past this hurdle then they can begin to allow help to heal as long as they don’t terminate their treatment/help; which does happen a lot.

​Secondly, extreme narcissists have to be willing to enter the realm of their childhood feelings again. They have been the masters of covering and hiding, even to themselves.  They now have to start uncovering these early painful wounds.  They have taught themselves to stuff and disconnect their feelings for years. Because of this, they tend to live inside their heads, in the realm of fantasy. This domain is a realm they feel they can control.  It is devoid of feelings especially for others. The realm of the heart or feelings is very intimidating and unsafe to them because it is non-linear and there is very little control of the outcomes. 
 
If extreme narcissists can overcome these two hurdles then there is much hope for them. They are on their road to healing.  However, it is very important to not reinforce their pathologic beliefs.  They have been in denial for years and it is a must to keep showing them the reality of things and speak only truth to them.  Understand, they can wear you out by being cruel when you speak truth but ignoring their pathological behavior will only help them stay in denial.
 
In conclusion, here is the Christian perspective:
Jesus can heal.  This person must go back to childhood wounds and face them but also know that Jesus will help them change if they allow Him to.  They need very close accountability for a while to help them stay on the path of truth so they will not go back to the lies and habits they have believed in the past.  They also must stretch themselves and begin to be giving emotionally to others, especially the ones closest to themselves and not expecting a payback.  As children, the ones closest to them were the most emotionally dangerous so they have “labeled” ALL their closest relationships as dangerous.  This is a lie.
If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves and pray
and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways,
then I will hear from heaven and I will forgive their sin and will heal their land.
​
2 Chronicles 7:14

​​HEART TO HEART: HOPE & HEALING

Welcome to the Heart to Heart Narcissistic and Emotional Abuse & Insecure Attachments Support Group Page, a compassionate, faith-centered community for those who have experienced narcissistic and emotional abuse, unhealthy relationship patterns, and attachment wounds.

If you have spent years feeling confused, unheard, emotionally exhausted, or questioning yourself because of a difficult relationship, you are not alone. Narcissistic abuse can deeply affect the way we see ourselves, trust others, establish boundaries, and experience relationships. Attachment wounds—often beginning much earlier in life—can influence whom we are drawn to, how we respond to closeness or conflict, and why certain relationship patterns seem to repeat themselves.

This group was created to provide a safe and supportive place to begin to understand those patterns and move toward healing.

Why This Support Group?

Narcissistic abuse can be especially isolating because much of what happens within the relationship may be invisible to everyone else.

Over time, manipulation, blame, criticism, emotional withdrawal, gaslighting, control, or repeated cycles of affection and rejection can leave a person wondering:

Was it really abuse?
Why did I stay?
Why do I still miss them?
Why do I keep questioning myself?
Why am I afraid to trust again?
​Why do I keep ending up in similar relationships?

Understanding narcissistic abuse is an important part of healing, but sometimes we also need to understand our own attachment patterns.

Our earliest relationships can influence how we experience love, safety, rejection, abandonment, intimacy, and conflict as adults. Recognizing these patterns is not about blaming ourselves for what happened. It is about gaining understanding so that the past no longer determines the future.

What You'll Find Here

Our group provides a confidential and compassionate environment where we can talk honestly about narcissistic abuse, attachment wounds, boundaries, emotional triggers, relationship patterns, rebuilding self-trust, healthy communication, grief, forgiveness, faith, and learning how to form healthier connections.
​
There is no expectation that everyone will be at the same place in their journey.
Some may still be trying to understand what is happening in their relationship. Others may have recently left. Some may have been out of the relationship for years but are realizing that certain wounds remain.

Wherever you are in that process, you are welcome here.
This is a place to learn, share, listen, grow, and heal alongside people who understand.
Above all, my hope is that you begin to recognize that what happened to you does not have to define the rest of your story.
Click Here for More Information on our Support Group
There is hope.
There is healing.

And there is life beyond unhealthy relationship patterns.

Welcome to Heart to Heart—a place where healing begins with understanding 
and where you don't have to walk the journey alone.
